items.title: Nirvana is not heaven — it is the cessation of craving
items.claim: How does Buddhism understand nirvana (nibbana in Pali)?

options.text: The 'blowing out' of the fires of greed, hatred and delusion — the end of suffering and rebirth, attainable in this life as well as at death (parinirvana)
A meditative trance state achieved daily

items.reveal:
The Pali 'nibbana' / Sanskrit 'nirvana' literally means 'blowing out' — as a flame is extinguished. The image is from the Adittapariyaya Sutta (Fire Sermon).

Nirvana attained in life is sometimes distinguished from parinirvana — the full nirvana at death of an enlightened being. The Buddha attained nirvana under the Bodhi tree (around age 35) and parinirvana around age 80.

The Buddha refused to speculate about nirvana's metaphysical status — whether the enlightened being exists, doesn't exist, both or neither after death (Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta). Speculation does not lead to liberation.
items.why: Translating nirvana as 'heaven' imports Christian assumptions. The Buddhist concept is structurally different — not a destination but an end, not a reward but a release.

items.title: Modern Judaism has three or four main branches
items.claim: What are the main Jewish denominations?

options.text: One unified Judaism with no internal divisions

Orthodox (including Modern Orthodox and Haredi); Conservative (called Masorti in UK); Reform; Reconstructionist — distinguished mainly by their stance on the binding nature of Halakhah (Jewish law) and the role of modernity
Only ethnic, not religious, divisions exist

items.reveal:
Reform Judaism emerged in early 19th-century Germany (Israel Jacobson, Abraham Geiger), arguing for adapting tradition to modern reason. Orthodox responses (Samson Raphael Hirsch) defended strict observance of Halakhah while engaging with modern life.

Conservative/Masorti Judaism (Zacharias Frankel, Solomon Schechter at JTS New York from 1902) is a middle path — Halakhah binding but historically developing. Reconstructionist Judaism (Mordecai Kaplan, 1922) sees Judaism as evolving religious civilisation.

In Israel, the Chief Rabbinate is Orthodox and controls marriage and conversion law; in the US, Reform is the largest denomination by membership.
items.why: Religions are internally diverse. Judaism's denominational landscape sets up the central modern question — how do tradition and modernity relate? — in different ways.

items.title: The Four Noble Truths are framed like a medical diagnosis
items.claim: What are the Four Noble Truths of Buddhism?

options.text: Dukkha (suffering exists), Samudaya (its cause is craving/tanha), Nirodha (it can cease), Magga (the path — the Eightfold Path)
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort

items.reveal:
The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths in his first sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) at Sarnath, near Varanasi, after his enlightenment. They are structured as a medical diagnosis: symptom, cause, prognosis, treatment.

'Dukkha' is often translated 'suffering' but covers unsatisfactoriness — the inability of conditioned things to give lasting peace. 'Tanha' is craving, including for existence and non-existence.

The Eightfold Path is grouped into wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, action, livelihood) and mental discipline (right effort, mindfulness, concentration).
items.why: Buddhism is often summarised as 'life is suffering' — a misleading reduction. The Four Noble Truths are a structured argument from problem to solution, not a pessimistic mood.
